subject: surgery
title: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome, Gangrene and Amputation

steps.tx: Compression of nerves and vessels between neck and armpit causes **thoracic outlet syndrome**. Extra cervical ribs or fibrous bands narrow the passage. Arm pain, tingling and hand weakness follow, worse when the arm is raised. Adson test, feeling the radial pulse fade as the head turns, is suggestive but positive in many normal people too.
steps.say: Thoracic outlet syndrome compresses nerves and vessels at the neck, worsening when the arm rises.

steps.tx: Most thoracic outlet cases are neurogenic and improve with **physiotherapy first**. Posture correction and scalene stretching relieve compression without surgery. Operation is reserved for persistent disabling symptoms or vascular damage. Ninety percent of neurogenic cases settle without surgery, so an operation offered at first visit should prompt a second opinion.
steps.say: Most thoracic outlet syndrome is neurogenic and improves with physiotherapy before any surgery.

steps.tx: An extra rib arising from the lowest neck vertebra is a **cervical rib**. It lifts the subclavian artery and plexus over a hard edge. Many cervical ribs cause no symptoms and are incidental findings. Cervical ribs occur in under one percent of people, are commoner in women, and are bilateral in about half of cases.
steps.say: A cervical rib lifts vessels and nerves over a hard edge, though many cause no symptoms.

steps.tx: Arterial damage at the outlet can shower clots into the hand, causing **digital emboli**. Fingers become painful and mottled in patches. Treating the outlet compression stops further embolisation. A subclavian artery aneurysm behind the narrowing is the usual source, and it needs repair, not just rib removal.
steps.say: Digital emboli from outlet arterial damage mottles fingers painfully until compression is relieved.

steps.tx: Removal of the first rib to widen the outlet is **first rib resection**. It decompresses nerves and vessels definitively in selected cases. Physiotherapy continues after surgery to restore shoulder movement. Pneumothorax and injury to the brachial plexus or long thoracic nerve are the complications patients must hear about beforehand.
steps.say: First rib resection widens the thoracic outlet definitively in selected persistent cases.

steps.tx: Dead tissue declares a boundary problem, and this step is about managing the border honestly. **Gangrene care** begins with keeping dry necrosis dry, protecting it from maceration and infection while the circulation is assessed for any salvageable inflow. Wet gangrene reverses every rule, becoming a surgical emergency where infected dead tissue seeds sepsis by the hour. Between those poles lie analgesia, glycaemic control, offloading and honest conversations about amputation levels, all timed so that demarcation guides the knife rather than panic doing so.
steps.say: Gangrene care keeps dry necrosis protected, treats wet gangrene as an emergency, and times amputation to demarcation.

steps.tx: Dead tissue at the limb end from any cause is managed by the principles of **gangrene care**. Infection is controlled, blood supply optimised and dead tissue removed at the right time. Premature amputation through inflamed tissue fails to heal. Dry gangrene is given time to declare its level, while wet gangrene is drained and debrided the same day.
steps.say: Gangrene care controls infection, optimises flow, and times removal where healing is possible.

steps.tx: Autoamputation, where dead toes separate naturally, occasionally suits frail patients with dry **demarcated gangrene**. It avoids anaesthesia when disease is stable and painless. Wet infected gangrene never qualifies for this approach. It can take months for a toe to separate, so pain, smell and the patient ability to cope decide whether waiting is humane.
steps.say: Dry demarcated gangrene in frail patients may autoamputate, but wet infected gangrene never qualifies.

steps.tx: Rehabilitation after major amputation centres on early **prosthetic fitting**. A well healed, well shaped stump accepts a prosthesis sooner. Physiotherapy, pain control and psychological support all begin before surgery. Fitting within the first month improves the chance of walking again, and stump shaping with rigid dressings speeds it.
steps.say: Early prosthetic fitting after amputation needs a well shaped stump plus pain and psychological support.

steps.tx: The pain that outlives the limb is the strangest entry in the amputee's chart. **Neuropathic pain** after amputation splits into stump pain from neuromas and phantom pain felt in a foot that no longer exists, two mechanisms sharing one clinic appointment. Early fitting, desensitisation and mirror therapy retrain the brain's map, while medicines borrowed from epilepsy and depression calm ectopic firing. Teams that warn patients beforehand, and treat early, spare them the fear that phantom sensations mean something has gone wrong.
steps.say: Neuropathic and phantom pain follow amputation, eased by early fitting, desensitisation and adjuvant medicines.

steps.tx: Phantom limb pain after amputation is managed with medicines for **neuropathic pain**. Gabapentinoids, mirror therapy and desensitisation help most patients. Reassurance that phantom sensation is normal reduces distress greatly. Pain that burns and shoots, with sensitivity to light touch, fits neuropathic pain and responds poorly to ordinary opioids.
steps.say: Phantom limb pain responds to neuropathic medicines, mirror therapy and clear reassurance.
